paragraphs.text: The Life of James the Monk, Full of Deep Compunction. Many blessings and virtuous deeds beneficial to the soul, for those beginning to live according to the Savior’s commandments, are brought about by the good acquisition of humility. Anyone who strives to acquire this and succeeds will not be subject to any fall, captivity to sin, or pride in his own confidence. For the great harm, unbearable injury, and great trouble that this brings upon those who are not watchful can be seen from many other signs, and particularly from the account that we are about to present, for the building up and strengthening of this angelic way of life. For in it we find both great self-restraint in life and the attainment of humility, great fasting, a subsequent fall through negligence

that befell him, and the power of repentance, which is so mighty before God, who loves mankind, that not only from the very gates of hell, but even from the fiery [?] and torment, it snatches a person away. And even greater goodness of character than before it is able to reveal, and, by the Lord’s grace, greater progress on his part. There was a certain hermit named James in the [?] city called Porphyrion. Having renounced this brief and empty life, he lived in a certain cave for fifteen years. He made such progress in fasting and good deeds that he proved worthy of honor and pleasing to God, so that he received the gift of power over demons and of performing many other healings in the name of our Christ. Everyone marveled at the man’s way of life and gathered around him. Most of them belonged to the faith of the lawless Samaritans. When the man of God saw them coming to him, he instructed them at length from the divine Scriptures and converted them to the true faith. But the devil, who has fought against the human race from the beginning, and especially against the servants of Christ our Savior, saw that he was being driven far away by the man’s many good deeds and righteous life, and rose against him, wishing to drive him from the place mentioned above. For he entered one of the Samaritans. of those who turn away from the truth from the beginning and continually. He prompted him to gather all who obeyed him—friends, relatives, and servants— to slander the holy man, so that, having ensnared him, he could drive him out of that region. They all gathered at the house of their priest, and after much deliberation and scheming,

they finally agreed on a single plan. They summoned a shameless and immoral woman and gave her twenty gold coins, promising to give her as much again if she could ensnare James, the servant of God, so that on that pretext they could drive the man out of their land in disgrace. Won over by these promises, the woman went to him very late at night. She knocked on the door and begged him to let her in. But he was unwilling and kept putting off doing so for a long time. She shamelessly persisted in knocking and earnestly pleading with him to take her in. He opened the door a little, and when he saw her, he thought she was an apparition. He made the sign of the cross over himself, shut and bolted the door, and went back. Standing facing east, he fervently offered prayer to God. Much time passed, and it was already the middle of the night, but she did not stop knocking and crying out in a loud voice, “Have mercy on me, servant of God, lest I be devoured by wild beasts before your very eyes!” The righteous man considered this, knowing that there were many wild beasts in those parts. After some hesitation, he opened the door and said to her, “Where have you come here from? Whom are you looking for?” She said, “I am from the monastery nearby, and the abbess sent me to bring a loaf of Eucharistic bread to this village. As I was returning and making my way to the monastery, night overtook me in this place. So I beg you, man of God, have mercy on me and take me in, so that I will not be devoured by wild beasts.”

Then, moved with compassion, he brought her inside and set water and bread before her. He himself went into the inner cell and locked himself in, leaving the woman in the outer cell. After eating, she remained quiet for a short time. Then she began to cry out and threw herself against the door, weeping. With bitter tears she called to the holy man. He leaned toward the door, and, seeing her in distress and apparently suffering great pain, he was at a loss. He asked her what would become of her or what he should do for her. She said to him, “Look after me and make the sign of the cross over me, for I am suffering from pain in my heart.” Hearing this, he went out, immediately built a large fire, and placed his left hand in the fire. With his right hand he anointed her with oil of the saints, warming her with the warmth of his hand. He did not stop repeatedly making the sign of the cross over her breast. She, enduring her shame, and wishing to ensnare him and lead the holy man into evil desire, said to him, “I beg you, keep anointing my heart for a long time, so that the pain afflicting me may stop.” In his simplicity, he did for her what would bring healing. Yet he also knew the tricks of the evil one and feared that, through his great concern for her, he might bring on an undying sickness. For two or three hours, he endured in this way, mercilessly holding his left hand to the fire, until the joints of his fingers burned through and fell off. He did this to resist Satan’s schemes, so that, through the unbearable pain that grew in him from the fire,

no evil thought would enter his heart. When she saw this astonishing thing, she came to her senses. For she saw that the holy man’s hand had already been completely burned by the fire. Weeping bitterly and sighing, she fell at the holy man’s feet. Beating her breast with her hands, she cried out, “Oh, woe to me, wretched and darkened as I am! Oh, woe to me, for I am food for the eternal fire! Oh, woe to me, for I am the devil’s dwelling place!” The holy man, alarmed at this, said to her, “Rise, woman.” With great difficulty he raised her from the ground and prayed earnestly. He said to her, “Tell me what is wrong with you.” When she finally came to herself, she told him what had happened, explaining everything to him and exposing the wicked Samaritans to him, and above all Satan’s plotting and attack against the righteous man. Immediately the servant of God sighed deeply, and, after thanking God at length with praise and tears, he instructed her in the faith. He then gave her loaves of offering bread. And he sent her to the holy bishop Alexander. When she reached the church, she confessed everything in order, first to God and then to the venerable man. He, in turn, gave her much instruction and found her earnestly repenting of the evil things she had done, and he gave her the bath of immortality. Then he sent the woman to a convent. Gathering all the God-loving people and the Christ-loving clergy, he drove all the Samaritans who were found there out of the city and the surrounding region. Then he came to James, the servant of God, and, strengthening him greatly like his own father,

he instructed him. The woman mentioned earlier was brought so close to Christ through repentance that she showed herself honorable [?] and was deemed worthy of the gift of power over demons. After a long time, the daughter of a certain councilor, tormented by an unclean demon, cried out, calling upon the saint. Her parents brought her to the servant of God and begged him to have mercy on her and drive the unclean demon out of her. When the saint had prayed and laid his hands on her, he immediately drove out the demon by the Lord’s grace and healed the girl. Her parents thanked God and then sent him three hundred gold coins. The righteous man not only refused to take them, but would not even look at them. He admonished them, telling them not to make God’s gift a matter of buying and selling. Instead, he told them, “Give them to the poor. I will not take this, for I live in the wilderness and have no need of these things.” Thus he sent them home giving thanks. On another occasion, a certain young man, overpowered by a demon, became paralyzed in both legs. His relatives picked him up and brought him to the saint, begging him to pray for him. He fasted for three days and devoted himself to prayer alone, and made the paralyzed man well. After blessing him, he told him to walk home on his own feet. Many others also came to him, suffering from various ailments, and all went away healed by the Lord’s grace. But when the servant of God saw that everyone held him in great honor, and saw the downfall that honor brings upon many, he left that place and fled about forty stadia from that city.

He found a large rocky cave in the riverbank. For thirty years he lived there, spending all his days and nights in prayers and hymns. For a long time he had fed on the plants growing in the river. Then he made a small garden on the bank and worked in it for a few hours of the day. From this he obtained his food. His way of life became so renowned that twenty or thirty monks at a time would come to him, as well as clergy and many laypeople, to receive his blessing and instruction. But this man, great and distinguished as he was, who had been deemed worthy of so great a gift, was soon seized by a certain conceit or pride and was allowed to fall into sin—and into the worst sin of all. For the utterly foul enemy of the human race, who always attacks those who live well in God, raging in his envy, entered a young girl, the daughter of a certain rich man, and began to cry out and call upon the holy man by name. Thus the girl's parents were compelled to travel about and search everywhere for the man of God, leaving no monastery or deserted place unsearched. When they could not find him, they later learned that a certain hermit was living in that place. Her father took his servants and made ready the girl and her mother in a [?]. He came to the place he had been told about, where the holy man was. Seeing him, he fell at his feet, saying, “Have mercy on my daughter, for she is being cruelly tormented by an unclean demon. It is now twenty

days since she has tasted either food or drink, and she cries out and tears at herself and calls upon your name.” The holy man told him to bring the girl before him. He gave himself to prayer and prayed so fervently that even the place where he stood shook. When he had finished praying, he blew upon the unclean spirit and said to it, “In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, come out of her.” Immediately the demon, driven out by fire, came out of the girl. She fell to the ground and for many hours lay without a sound. The holy man prayed, took her by the hand, raised her up, and returned her to her parents in good health. When they saw the miracle, they glorified God. But fearing that the unclean spirit might return and enter her, they begged him to let the girl stay with him for two days, until she was completely freed from the demon. They left her with him and returned to their home. It was fitting, as we also said in the introduction, for the strengthening and building up of those who live this angelic life. not only to recount the achievements of those who are perfect. gathering only what is good from these things, so that they may remain untempted and unharmed by the malicious snares of the utterly foul enemy of God’s servants. But just as we have described the man’s great and truly good character, so we must also recount the storm that struck him and the great fall that befell him as a result. Then we shall tell what happened afterward, as it truly was, and, following his complete repentance and courageous confession, the exceedingly great miracles. For however great the self-restraint and way of life he had previously

shown, so very far did he fall away. And however great his fall, so much greater afterward was his restoration. For the utterly deceitful and unclean enemy of God’s servants, seeing that the girl who had been healed had been left there alone, immediately rose against the righteous man and attacked him with a demon of lust, so as to overpower him in this way. Thus a man such as this, who at the beginning of his way of life, when caught in the snare of the ungodly Samaritans, being tempted by the woman mentioned above, had resisted and overcome her, and had endured an injury to his left hand, trampling down the devil who had sent her, fell into burning lust and forgot the fear of God and the great gift of healing given to him, and his self-restraint over so many years and his many labors; and, although he had already reached old age, he did not endure the struggle, but went out to the outskirts of the city to lie with the girl and defile himself with the mire of lawlessness. From then on, as though the demon had been given an opening, he urges him to add to the first a second evil. For the destructive serpent, fearing the repentance granted by [?] to those who seek him wholeheartedly for their restoration, presses him, as one whom he already considered his own captive, to add a greater act of lawlessness than the first. For, having sown a thought to terrify him, he incites him to kill the girl whom he had violated. Defeated in this too, he murdered her, wishing to escape her parents’ punishment, as he thought, by doing this. But the enemy was not satisfied even with these defilements,

that original evil one, Satan; for to defilement he adds murder, and to murder. not only to consign the murdered woman’s body to the grave, but also to have it mercilessly thrown into the river waters and to wild beasts and birds. Such is the fruit of pride and of thinking too highly of oneself. For if he had not enslaved himself to any passion, the wicked enemy would not have been able to shatter his conscience against a rock, as though in a leaky boat. For the enemy gained power in old age over the man who in his youth had conquered all the force and spirit of lust. But this man thought too highly of himself, and the wicked one defeated him. Nevertheless, Christ, who bestows great gifts, in his exceedingly great love for humanity, desiring the salvation of all people rather than their destruction, offered a hand to the prisoner who lay fallen, and the healing herb of repentance, and healed the incurable, foul-smelling sores of his own creature. And the man became worthy of the same and even greater gifts after his repentance. I was compelled to set these things before everyone, so that, just as we glorified God when we first learned of his life, and fell into sorrow when we learned how he had fallen, so, on learning of the man’s earnest repentance, we may place our hope not in ourselves but in the loving God who gives us gifts. When we stand, he will give us the endurance to stand firm to the end, and when we fall through negligence, he strengthens us, extending his helping hand to us. And when we repent, he receives us according to his own love for humanity.

For he had committed so many and such great evils, each of which made him the fiery [?]’s food. Having as his guide blessed David, who regained his standing after going astray, and who, instead of receiving judgment for adultery, added even the murder of the man who suffered that calamity, and considering how, satisfied with a mere word, the loving Master immediately granted him forgiveness for such great sins, he seeks refuge in the peace of repentance, having hope alone as his guide toward setting his soul right. For he came to his senses and entered his cell, as though awakening from sleep, as one might say. Throwing himself on the ground, he let out unbearable groans, beating his chest without mercy and pouring out a fountain of tears. But even so, he did not leave him. the unclean and defiled demon. For the devil, unable even to look upon the man's resolve, sows thoughts of despair in him—that source of evil for the human race, having found [?] through Judas's despair. Then he rose from the ground and rushed out into the world. By the will of God, who loves humankind, it happened that, as he went along, he came to a monastery. He went in to the brothers who were there and greeted them. They washed his feet and set bread before him, urging him to eat. But he would not even hear of it. Sighing bitterly, he said, “Oh, woe to me, wretched as I am! How can I look up to heaven? How can I dare to call upon the name of Christ the Master, whom I have denied and abandoned? How can I hope to receive any of his blessings, when I have strayed from him in soul and body and defiled myself with adultery and murder?” And he began to confess,

telling them everything that had happened, just as it truly was. They were deeply saddened and concerned about his many troubles, and comforted him as best they could. They gave him a blessing, prayed earnestly for him, and sent him on his way. As he was traveling along the road, a certain brother met him who truly had Christ within him. He prevailed upon him and brought him into his cell. He washed his feet and showed him every kindness, set bread before him, and offered many prayers. He urged him to partake of the blessings God had sent. But the man was tormented by his conscience and would not bring himself to partake at all. The servant of God threw himself at his feet, begging him and swearing that he would not rise from the ground unless he first promised to taste what had been set before him. When he had promised, the man of God raised him from the ground. They prayed, and both sat down to eat bread. After they had eaten and finished giving thanks, they sat down again. And approaching the man, the brother who had received him into his dwelling said to him, “Father, instruct me, your son in Christ, and strengthen my heart, for various thoughts have a powerful hold on me.” Then the holy man cried out, and with tears and sighs beat his breast, saying, “Forgive me, brother.” to repent and weep for my great sins and for the lawless deeds I have dared to commit against God. For in these vain and dishonored gray hairs of mine, like a little child tripped up by the devil,

I descended into utter ruin. For the evils that I had endured throughout my life and overcome—into these I fell in my old age by doing evil, throwing myself into the stinking mire of sexual sin and defiling myself with other sins greater than that. Hearing this, the other man was deeply grieved. And he begged him to recount [?] the whole deception of Satan. The holy man sought two benefits for himself: first, hoping through confession to lead him back, and at the same time wishing to make it a safeguard for himself against what might come afterward. He answered and said to him: After I had practiced true and very arduous abstinence, after I had served God blamelessly for eight years, after I had received a great gift from God, who loves humankind, after great miracles had been performed by me, defiled as I am, Satan finally entered a certain young woman. Then her parents, having heard of the Lord’s gift within me, immediately brought her to me to be healed. At their request, I prayed for her, and immediately, by the Lord’s grace, the unclean spirit departed from her. But wishing her to be healed more completely, they left her with me for two days and went home. But with my conscience darkened, I went out to her, and the burning of lust overcame me. At that moment I neither brought God to mind nor considered the loss of so much abstinence and labor or gave it any weight. Forgetting everything, so to speak, and disregarding the river of fire, I fell into the ruin

of sexual sin. And after committing sexual sin with her, I sought to cure evil with evil, or rather, added an even greater evil to evil. For the demon of shamelessness seized me and advised me to murder her. And after sinning sexually with her, I killed her and threw her into the river. And despairing of my salvation, I went away. And now I am going into the world. For how can I look up on high, or even dare to name Christ? Will fire not immediately descend and burn me up? These things, and many more than these, he said to him. as the man confessed with many tears and unbearable sighs. When the servant of God heard this, he was moved by grace, fell on his neck, and kissed him, saying: “Do not grieve too much, brother, or despair of your salvation, but believe that there is salvation. Approach with tears and confess to God, who loves humanity, for very compassionate and most merciful is God, and great is his mercy toward us. So let us repent while we have time. For if there were no repentance, how could David, after receiving the gift of prophecy, after becoming king, and after the Lord’s testimony about him, have fallen into the pit of adultery and murder, expressed his repentance in words, and received forgiveness for such great sins? How could blessed Peter, the foremost of the apostles, the first disciple, who received the keys of heaven from the Lord, Christ the Master, have denied him not once or twice, but three times, and afterward wept bitterly, and not only received forgiveness for such a sin, but also been counted worthy of greater honor, becoming a shepherd to the Master’s rational sheep?

If there were no repentance, how could Paul, after repenting, have become a chosen vessel instead of a persecutor? If there were no repentance, how could Paul have commanded that the man among the Corinthians who had committed sexual immorality be received back, saying, ‘So that we may not be overpowered and plundered by Satan’?” With these and similar words, the true and merciful brother greatly strengthened his heart and begged him to stay with him. But when he refused, the man of God fell down before him and kissed his feet, begging him not to leave him. For he was thinking with fear that, if the man remained in despair, he might utterly destroy his soul. And although he urged him at length, pleading, falling before him, and bowing down, he could not persuade him. The holy man grieved and sighed in his spirit, and after praying earnestly, he blessed him and let him go on his way. Yet he accompanied him for fifteen stadia and did not stop pleading with him. After speaking to him at length about repentance, he embraced him and kissed him with tears, and, having prayed for him, returned to his cell. James took the road leading into the world and continued his journey. After traveling some distance and turning a little aside, he found an old tomb resembling a cave, in which lay many bones of the dead that had crumbled over many years. And entering it, he gathered the bones and placed them in one corner. And he shut himself in the cave, closing it with the old doors that lay over it. And bending his knees, he confessed to God, mercilessly beating

his breast. And with weeping and much sobbing he said: “How shall I look toward you, O God? What beginning shall I find for my confession? With what heart, or with what hope, or with what conscience shall I dare to move my impious tongue and my lips, full of defilement? How shall I attempt it? And first, for which sin shall I dare to ask forgiveness? Have mercy, O Lord who loves humankind. Be merciful to me, unworthy as I am, O good Master. And do not destroy me because of my shameless deeds, for my transgressions are not small. I committed fornication. I committed murder. I shed innocent blood. And in addition to all these things, I gave that body which had suffered to the waters and to beasts and birds to be eaten. And now, O Lord, I confess everything to you, the good one who knows all things, asking forgiveness for it. Do not disregard me, O Master, but according to your gracious mercy, have mercy on me, impious as I am. And send upon me the great mercy that comes from you, and forgive me all my transgressions, so that, having sunk into the depths of sin, I may not be utterly destroyed by the storm of the destructive enemy, nor may the serpent of the depths devour me.” And with such great repentance, he continued confessing for ten years in that cave—or rather, I should say, in that tomb—without leaving the place, conversing with no one, speaking to no one, but with bitter tears and unbearable sighing, and with deep contrition, he spent all that time, opening the little door twice a week, finding grass growing before the doors of his tomb,

and crushing it, he ate as much as was sufficient for him, tasting it; and immediately he returned with much praise, devoting himself always to prayer and self-restraint and to [?] confession. Therefore God, who loves humankind and desires not the death of sinners but their repentance and life, did not allow such suffering and great hardship to continue uselessly or in vain. For he knew his sincere and profound repentance, through which he had received forgiveness for sins so numerous and so grievous. And he wished to reassure the holy man himself and to reveal to everyone the power of repentance. While a fierce storm and a prolonged drought gripped that land, with many prayers and processions the people prayed. It was revealed to the devout bishop of that city, a holy man who truly feared God, that there was a certain father in the burial ground at that place, humble in appearance but good in spirit, who, if he listened to them and prayed to God, would put an end to all the calamities that had fallen upon that land. Then that holy bishop commanded all his clergy to assemble to hear the account of that revelation and to go with crosses to the cave where the man of God lived. When this had been done and they had reached the place, he found that holy, righteous man and earnestly begged him to have mercy on their land and to pray to God that he would have mercy on his people, drive away the drought that afflicted them, and send rain upon their land. But the holy man gave no answer [?], and beat his

breast, not daring even to look up to heaven, and said, “Be merciful, Lord, concerning my many wicked deeds.” Although the bishop waited and entreated him, he received not even a brief answer. Leaving him, they went away weeping. When they reached the holy church, they immediately prayed there with tears and asked God, who loves humankind, for deliverance from that calamity. For many days, with fasting and weeping, they called upon God to come to their aid. And immediately he appeared to that same bishop, who heard a voice [?] saying to him, “Go to my servant Jacob, whom I revealed to you before, and ask him to pray for whatever you wish. When he has prayed, you will be delivered from the calamities afflicting the land.” Then the holy bishop of God quickly returned again with all the clergy and the people. [?] concerning the entreaty addressed to Jacob, the man of God. Then, at that very time, unwillingly, so to speak, having been persuaded by many entreaties and urged by the holy man, just as before, so now they had come to him through a revelation from God. He raised his eyes to heaven and prayed earnestly for a long time. And while the prayer was still on his lips, the good and merciful God, who generously and readily gives all things to those who fear him, fulfilling in deed the written word which says, “While you are still speaking, behold, I have come,” sent abundant rain down upon the earth. Amazed at this, with a hymn of praise to his mercy and ineffable majesty, they departed, glorifying God

and calling his servants blessed. Through their self-restraint and hunger, they had been deemed worthy of so great a gift. Having received this great blessing from God, who loves mankind, and having escaped the plague that had come upon them by God's permission, which was driven away by the prayer of Jacob, the servant of God, every year to this very day they commemorate that day on which they were freed from the calamities of the weather, offering hymns of prayer and praise to Christ the Lord. Many who were suffering from various afflictions, from among the people who had come to him, who had come together with the bishop for prayer, were left with Jacob, the servant of God, to be healed. The holy man took oil and blessed them, anointed them in Christ's name, and healed them, so that, as they went home [?], they glorified and blessed God, who had granted them healing through his servant. Then all those who lived in the city and in the surrounding villages brought their sick to him, and as they departed, they begged him to pray for their salvation, and immediately they received healing by the Lord's grace. For so great a gift was given to him that he could quickly drive out unclean spirits with a word. One year after that terrible plague had been driven away, Jacob, the servant of God, summoned the holy bishop and asked him to take care of the cave, that is, the tomb, in which the holy man lived, and begged him with earnest prayer. to bury him in it after his death. When the other man had promised him this

and returned to the city, a few days later blessed James died at a good old age, being seventy-five years old. When the venerable bishop learned of this, he came to that place with all the clergy and with the ascetic [?]. Having wrapped him with costly spices, singing and praising God, they laid his honored body in that tomb. Afterward, the venerable bishop, a man of God, built a house of prayer, that is, a church, near the cave and transferred his honored body there. In that place many healings take place to this day. The whole city and the villages surrounding it commemorate him every year with a great festival, to the glory of God, who honored him and loves mankind. We too glorify him according to the established order, blessing the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, to whom belong glory and dominion, now and always and throughout the endless ages of ages. Amen.
